answer.why: As an insider, 'Confirmed & Substantive' made me laugh straight away because it is exactly the phrase you wait years to see on your appointment letter, and it tells me the developer actually knows the service. 'Minister Salary' is the headline everyone outside already argues about, so it feels like clickbait, though I would probably tap it out of professional curiosity and to check whether they got the benchmarking right.
answer.expect_minister_salary: A satirical or political game about the ministerial pay debate, probably with a gotcha tone: climb the ladder, get rich, get criticised online. I would expect broad strokes, a bit of cynicism, and the benchmark formula wrong or oversimplified. It would sell better, but I would brace for a cartoon version of my job.
answer.expect_confirmed_substantive: A quieter, drier, more insider game about the slow grind of civil service life: probation, confirmation, acting appointments versus substantive ones, appraisals, waiting for the promotion board. I would expect humour in the wording and small details rather than big drama, and I would trust it more to get the grades and processes right. The risk is that outsiders would have no idea what it means, and it is a bit of a mouthful.

best_moment.what: The Minister used my ninth draft, and the AO I had taught plainly started to become someone who would remember it. It felt like how the service really works: quiet, unrecorded credit that pays off years later.

worst_moment.what: Learning that CEP was the undisclosed ceiling, then the repeated go-home-or-finish-clearance choices around it. The same dilemma kept coming back, and the pay header and package mismatch made the reward screens hard to trust.

skip_year.why: The rumour that there is no rung above Perm Sec was passive. I just read it and tapped through, and the real decision only came at Y21 to Y22.

answer.held_back_by: At the top it was REP, not competence. I had 48 when a single seat needed 60, so the visible public profile I never built mattered more than my 100 integrity and 99 competence. The game seems to say that excellence inside the service does not turn into votes.
answer.ending_fair_why: Losing at 48.2% is plausible, and the card's line that it was never about me matches how GRC teams work. It was a little thin for a 24-year run. The AO I was waiting for never came back after the loss, which I wanted to see.
answer.chase_next: The office-holder ending. I would build REP early, through the public-facing choices I skipped, to see whether a single seat or a stronger GRC slot opens up, and I would be curious whether the ceiling stays hidden.
answer.play_again_why: Mostly yes. The institutional detail is good and I want to know whether I can win with a different reputation path, but I would take a break first because the clearance and go-home dilemmas got repetitive.

tone_breaks.note: A GRC team contests a ward, but the card reads like a single-member fight. Minor. A GRC is a team contest and a party-level loss, which the second half of the line sort of acknowledges.

answer.title_fit_why: The best parts were appraisal wording, the quiet pilot, and the AO callback, which is the service's own language. Minister Salary pitches a payoff I never reached, and the run was about the grind of substantive appointments.
